title: Himachal Pradesh — Kangra and Chamba (Dharamshala, McLeodganj, Bir Billing, Palampur, Dalhousie, Khajjiar, Chamba, Bharmaur)
selection: Light first pass of the Kangra–Chamba region, chosen as the most-visited part of Himachal after Kullu-Manali: Dharamshala and McLeodganj, Bir Billing, Palampur, Dalhousie and Khajjiar, Chamba and Bharmaur, with their main attractions and experiences. Sources: Himachal Tourism's destination pages, District Kangra, and Wikipedia for Bir. Not found in any official source: opening hours and fees for Kangra Fort, Norbulingka, museums and temples; paragliding and Triund camping prices — shown as unconfirmed. Editor notes: Gaggal airport is 14 km (Himachal Tourism) or 13 km (District Kangra) from Dharamshala; Khajjiar distances differ slightly between the Dalhousie and Chamba pages — ranges are shown. Himachal Tourism dates Dalhousie to 1850 and an Akbar siege of Kangra Fort to 1615; neither date is used.

DS1.claim: Dharamshala lies below the Dhauladhar range; Kotwali Bazar and the markets around it form Lower Dharamshala.

evidence.quote: Lying in the shadow of mighty Dhauladhar range is the quaint town of Dharamshala.
Divided in two halves – Kotwali Bazar and the skirting markets make up Lower Dharamshala

DS2.claim: Dharamshala is an 18 km uphill drive from Kangra.

evidence.quote: It is an 18 km gradual uphill drive from Kangra that gets you to Dharamshala.

DS3.topic: Seat of the Tibetan government in exile
DS3.claim: McLeodganj is the seat of the Tibetan Government in exile; the 14th Dalai Lama came here after the 1959 uprising.

evidence.quote: Mcleodganj serves as the capital of the Tibetan Government in exile.
It was in the wake of the Tibetan uprising of 1959 that His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama escaped from Lhasa.

DS4.claim: Hindi, Punjabi and English are spoken in the tourism trade; locals speak Kangri and the Tibetan community speaks Tibetan.

evidence.quote: Hindi, Punjabi, English are understood and spoken by the people engaged in tourism trade. Natives speak Kangri and Tibetan is spoken by the immigrant Buddhist community.

DS5.claim: Lower Dharamshala is warmer in summer, while the upper town gets very cold in winter.

evidence.quote: Lower reaches of Dharamshala experience higher temperature in summers whereas the upper region gets really cold in winters.

DS6.claim: The best times are March to June and December to February, when snowfall is likely.

evidence.quote: Best time to visit Dharamshala is from March through June in the summer and from December through February in winter with there being a good chance of witnessing a snowfall.

DS7.claim: Kangra airport at Gaggal is 13–14 km from Dharamshala, with regular flights from Delhi.

evidence.quote: Kangra airport at Gaggal is at a distance of 14 km from Dharamshala. There are regular flights between Delhi and Kangra to this airport.
The nearest Airport is at Gaggal, 13 Kms from Dharamshala and 8 Kms from Kangra Town.

DS8.claim: The nearest broad-gauge station is Pathankot, about 94–95 km away; a narrow-gauge line runs from Pathankot to Kangra station, 20 km from Dharamshala.

evidence.quote: The nearest broad gauge railway line to Dharamshala is at Pathankot which is then connected by a 94 km narrow gauge line to Kangra.
The nearest railway station is at Kangra, 20 KMs from Dharamshala connected to Pathankot through narrow gauge line.

DS9.claim: Public and private buses run to Delhi, Chandigarh, Pathankot, Kullu-Manali and Shimla, and taxis are easy to find.

evidence.quote: Both public and private transport buses regularly ply between Dharamshala to Delhi, Chandigarh, Pathankot, Kullu-Manali, Shimla and other destinations. Taxis for all places are readily available.

DS10.claim: One road route from Delhi runs via Ambala, Ropar, Una and Kangra.

evidence.quote: This access route leads via Sonipat – Panipat – Karnal – Kurukshetra (Pipli)- Ambala – Zirakpur – Kharar – Ropar – Swarghat – Una – Amb – Mubarakpur – Dehra Gopipur – Ranital – Kangra – Gaggal – Dharamshala

DS11.claim: HRTC and HPTDC buses can be booked online on their websites.

evidence.quote: For online Bus Booking in HRTC buses please  visit HRTC website
For online Bus Booking in HPTDC buses  Please visit HPTDC website

DS12.claim: Public parking: Hotel Bhagsu car park and the McLeodganj car park upstairs, Community Hall parking in Kotwali Bazar.

evidence.quote: Parking Locations: Hotel Bhagsu Car Parking, Parking of Mcleodganj and Community Hall Parking, Kotwali Bazar.

DS13.claim: McLeodganj stands at 2,082 m; its main street has Tibetan craft shops and eateries with Tibetan flavours, and the market centres on the Tsuglagkhang.

evidence.quote: the suburb at an elevation of 2,082 m is also referred to as mini Lhasa
The main street of Mcleodganj is sprinkled with Tibetan craft shops and amazing eateries serving fresh and savoury dishes cooked with a tinge of Tibetan cooking flavours.
Major section of the market is centered around the Tsuglag Khang Temple

DS14.claim: Dharamkot, above McLeodganj, is home to many foreigners and is the base for the Triund trek.

evidence.quote: Dharamkot is home to many foreigners and life in this small village is influenced by western lifestyles. This village is also the base for a trek to Triund

DS15.claim: The Bhagsunag temple, 2 km from McLeodganj, has a spring-fed pool for a holy dip; the waterfall above is fullest from July to September.

evidence.quote: The spring water flows into a pool where pilgrims do take a holy dip. The temple at a walkable distance is just 2 kms from Mcleodganj.
The best time to be at the waterfall is in the rainy season from July to September when the stream is in full flow.

DS16.claim: St. John in the Wilderness, built in 1852 in a forest at Forsyth Ganj, has Belgian stained glass; Lord Elgin is buried in its grounds.

evidence.quote: was constructed in 1852 and is set in a forest at Forsythg Ganj
Within its compound lies buried Lord Elgin, a Viceroy from 1862-63. The church has some fine Belgian stained glass windows.

DS17.claim: The Kangra Art Museum in Kotwali Bazar shows more than 1,500 artefacts, some from the 5th century AD, and Kangra miniature paintings.

evidence.quote: At Kotwali Bazar is the Kangra Art Museum
On display are more than 1500 artefacts and crafts, some dating back to the 5th century AD. It also has a fine collection of miniature paintings.

DS18.claim: The War Memorial at the entrance to Dharamshala honours soldiers who died in service.

evidence.quote: is the War Memorial that pays tribute to the known and unknown soldier who have died in service of the nation.

DS19.claim: Norbulingka Institute at Sidhpur, 7 km from Dharamshala, was founded in 1995 to preserve Tibetan arts, crafts and culture.

evidence.quote: The institute was founded in 1995 by Kelsang and Kim Yeshi to preserve the Tibetan arts, crafts and culture. Norbulingka Institute at Sidhpur is 7 km from Dharamshala.
Streams running through well maintained Japanese styled gardens, birds fluttering about in trees and the vibrant Tibetan architecture of Norbulingka Institute

DS20.claim: Gyuto Monastery at Sidhwari near Dharamshala is the exile residence of the Karmapa.

evidence.quote: Dwelling place of the Karmapa, a highly revered Tibetan Lama, in exile, the Gyuto monastery at Sidhwari near Dharamshala.

DS21.claim: The Chamunda Devi temple is 15 km from Dharamshala and 24 km from Kangra and draws pilgrims all year.

evidence.quote: 15 km from Dharamshala, the Chamunda Devi temple is a place that draws a steady stream of pilgrims around the year.
Easy to reach, this highly revered temple is 15 km for Dharamshala and 24 km from Kangra.

DS22.claim: Most of the area's best eateries and restaurants are in and around McLeodganj.

evidence.quote: has some of the best eateries, restaurants and food joints, with most of them located in and around Mcleodganj.

DS23.claim: The government Zonal Hospital in Dharamshala handles emergencies; Tanda Medical College near Kangra has specialist care.

evidence.quote: The Government run Zonal Hospital in the city is equipped to meet any medical emergency that a tourist may face while visiting Dharamshala.
Facilities at the nearby Tanda Medical College, Kangra supplement the medical needs of those who need specialised care.

DS24.claim: A fair is held at the Dal Lake in Upper Dharamshala in August.

evidence.quote: the Dal fair in Upper Dharamshala in August is a big draw

DS25.claim: Triund (2,875 m) is a moderate trek through oak and deodar forest; the last stretch climbs 22 steep bends to an open camping ground.

evidence.quote: a summer trek to Triund (altitude 2875 meter), just below the snowline
Making way through thick oak and deodar forests with scattered rhododendron flowers in the path, this moderate trek
The last stretches of the trek are demanding as you make your way up the 22 gruelling curves to an open camping ground.

DS26.claim: Dal Lake, 4 km from McLeodganj, is a quiet picnic spot in a deodar forest.

evidence.quote: Dal Lake is 4 km from Mcleodganj, is a quiet picnic spot. The area has a deodar tree forest cover from all sides

DS27.claim: Beyond Triund, the demanding Indrahar Pass trek (4,342 m) from Galu Devi Temple near Dharamkot is done from April to October.

evidence.quote: Indrahar Pass at an altitude of 4,342 meters is a demanding trek from Galu Devi Temple near Dharamkot village, Dharamshala.
One can attempt to cross this pass that goes over some incredible terrain from April to October.

DS28.claim: The Tsuglagkhang temple complex is the centre of McLeodganj, with the market around it.

evidence.quote: Major section of the market is centered around the Tsuglag Khang Temple, bestowing good wishes on residents and tourists.

DS29.claim: Kareri Lake (2,934 m), fed by snowmelt, is a trekking destination in the Dhauladhars.

evidence.quote: At 2934 meters altitude, this mountain water body is a trekking destination in the Dhauladhars. Source of the shallow lakes water is snow melt.

KG1.claim: Kangra Fort, built by the Katoch rulers, is one of the largest and oldest forts in the Himalayas; the 1905 earthquake damaged it badly.

evidence.quote: One of the largest and the oldest forts in the Himalayas, Kangra Fort built by Katoch rulers dates back thousands of years.
It was the devastating earthquake of 1905 that caused extensive damage to it.

KG2.claim: The fort, also called Nagarkot, is about 3 km from Kangra town; a museum at the entrance has old photographs of the fort.

evidence.quote: The Kangra Fort is approximately 3 Km from the town and is also known as Nagarkot.
At the entrance is a museum containing some valuable old photographs of the fort

KG3.claim: The fort stands on high ground protected on three sides by the Banganga river and another stream.

evidence.quote: Built on a high ground that is naturally protected by River Banganga and another stream on three sides

KG4.claim: September to May is the best time for sightseeing around Kangra.

evidence.quote: Best time to visit Kangra is from September to May.

KG5.claim: Kangra is 10 km from Gaggal airport and on the Pathankot–Joginder Nagar narrow-gauge line; Delhi is 456 km by road.

evidence.quote: Kangra Airport at Gaggal is just 10 km from Kangra.
Kangra is connected by the Pathankot – Jogindernagar narrow gauge rail line.
Delhi – Kangra is 456 km

BR1.claim: Bir, among tea gardens, is a paragliding centre known for Buddhist monasteries and Tibetan handicrafts; Billing is 14 km above it.

evidence.quote: Sheltered by the mountains and surrounded by tea gardens, Bir (35km), serves as a playground for para-gliders and is well known for its Buddhist monasteries and Tibetan handicrafts.
Billing is 14 km from Bir.

BR2.claim: Bir-Billing is one of the world's best aero-sports sites and has hosted the paragliding world cup; cross-country flights run for over 200 km.

evidence.quote: One of the best aero sports sites in the world and a venue of the world para-gliding tournament.
Bir-Billing offers great opportunities for high altitude and cross-country para-gliding for a stretch of over 200 km.

BR3.claim: The main flying season is September and October, with some flying in November.

evidence.quote: The flying season is in September and October, with some flying in November.

BR4.claim: Flights take off from the meadow at Billing (about 2,400 m) and land at Chowgan, on the southern edge of Bir, where most stays are.

evidence.quote: at an elevation of 2400 meters
while the landing site and most tourist accommodations are in the village of Chowgan (also spelled Chaugan), on the southern edge of Bir.

BR5.claim: The Bir Tibetan Colony was founded in the early 1960s for refugees after the 1959 uprising.

evidence.quote: It is the location of the Bir Tibetan Colony , founded in the early 1960s as a settlement for Tibetan refugees after the 1959 Tibetan uprising .

BR6.claim: Chokling Gompa's Tibetan architecture and large stupa are the main sights; it has a guest house and restaurant.

evidence.quote: The Tibetan architecture and large stupa are the principal attractions for casual visitors.
There is a guest house and restaurant on the premises.

BR7.claim: Sherab Ling Monastery is a 50–70 minute walk or 15-minute taxi ride from Chowgan.

evidence.quote: Sherab Ling Monastery is a 50-to-70-minute walk (or 15-minute taxi) from Chowgan, or slightly longer from Upper Bir.

BR8.claim: The cooperative Bir Tea Factory offers tours of tea-making.

evidence.quote: The Bir Tea Factory is a long-standing Bir cooperative, which offers tours for those interested in the process of tea production.

BR9.claim: Ahju narrow-gauge station is 3 km away, Kangra airport 67 km and Pathankot (broad gauge) about 112 km.

evidence.quote: Ahju railway station, a narrow-gauge railway , is 3 kilometres away.
Kangra Airport is 67 kilometres away.
About 112 kilometres away is the broad gauge station at Pathankot

BR10.claim: Bir is reached from the signposted Bir Road turn-off on NH 154 between Baijnath and Joginder Nagar, about 50 km (two to three hours) from Dharamshala.

evidence.quote: Bir can be reached from the Bir Road turnoff (signposted) on NH 20 (now NH 154), approximately midway between Baijnath and Jogindernagar .
It is approximately 50 km (31 mi) south-east of Dharamshala at a distance of two to three hours by road.

BR11.claim: Hotels and homestays are in and around Bir and spreading to Damehar, Gunehar and Chauntra.

evidence.quote: with hotels and homestays located in and around the village and spreading towards other villages, including Damehar, Gunehar, and Chauntra .

BR12.claim: The Hanumangarh trek is a short trek near Bir-Billing.

evidence.quote: Hanumangarh Trek (also called Hanuman Garh Trek) is a beautiful and rewarding short trek near Bir-Billing in Kangra district

BR13.claim: Every year adventure activities, paragliding included, close for two months in the rains.

evidence.quote: Every year, adventure activities are closed for two months during the rainy season, and tourists have to wait for two months to participate in paragliding, river rafting, water sports, and other activities.

BR14.claim: Before paragliding or trekking, check the operator is government-authorised and licensed.

evidence.quote: Before taking part in any adventure activity such as trekking,rafting, paragliding, ensure the agencies offering such activities are authorized by the Government for the purpose and have a valid license to operate.

PL1.claim: Palampur, 35 km from Kangra, sits on a plateau by the Neugal chasm, among tea estates and pine and deodar forest.

evidence.quote: Palampur is 35 km from Kangra, is a quiet town situated on a plateau with the backdrop of the dramatic Neugal chasm and the Bundla stream cutting across on one edge.
Surrounded by green tea estates and forests of pine and deodar

PL2.claim: Palampur is known as the tea capital of North India; visitors can learn about tea making in its gardens.

evidence.quote: Known as the tea capital of North India, Palampur owes its tourism to these tea gardens where one can even catch up with the finer nuances of the tea making and brewing processes.

PL3.claim: Andretta, 13 km from Palampur, is known for the Sobha Singh art gallery and Norah Richards' pottery.

evidence.quote: Visit Andretta, a charming village which is 13km from Palampur and is famous for Sardar Sobha Singh Art gallery and Norah Richards pottery.

PL4.claim: The stone Shiva temple at Baijnath, 16 km from Palampur, was rebuilt by two merchants in 1204 AD.

evidence.quote: Visit ancient Shiva Temple at Baijnath, 16Km from Palampur.
the stone temple of Baijnath was rebuilt at an existing temple site by two local merchants in 1204 AD

PL5.claim: At Shivratri the temple is garlanded with flowers and a fair draws thousands of pilgrims.

evidence.quote: For Shivratri the temples is draped in flower garlands which enhances its beauty and grace.
Every year during the Shivratri fair, thousands of pilgrims descend on Baijnath to enjoy the colorful fair and festivities.

PL6.claim: A Holi fair is held in Palampur every February–March.

evidence.quote: Every year in Februry/March, Holi Fair is organized at Palampur

PL7.claim: Buses run from Dharamshala, Kangra, Kullu and Shimla; Palampur is on the Pathankot–Joginder Nagar narrow-gauge line; local buses and taxis get you around.

evidence.quote: By Road: Transport Buses from Dharamsala, Kangra, Kullu and Shimla.
By Rail: Pathankot-Jogindernagar narrow gauge railway line.
Local buses operate regularly. Taxis are also available

PL8.claim: Winters get quite cold and summers are hot: cottons in summer, heavy woollens in winter.

evidence.quote: In winter the temperature get quite low and summers are hot.
Cotton clothes in Summer and heavy woolens in winter.

PL9.claim: The steep trek to the Aadi Himani Chamunda temple at 2,900 m is for fit walkers only.

evidence.quote: At 2900 meters, a pilgrimage to the temple is only for the die-hards.

PL10.claim: Dhauladhar Nature Park is at Gopalpur, 15 km from Palampur.

evidence.quote: Visit Dhauladhar Nature Park at Gopalpur, 15km from Palampur Town.

PL11.claim: Bir-Billing's paragliding site is about 35 km from Palampur.

evidence.quote: paragliding at Bir-Billing 35 km away

DL1.claim: Dalhousie spreads over five hills and was founded by Lord Dalhousie as a summer retreat; it keeps colonial churches and a touch of Tibetan culture.

evidence.quote: Spread out over the five hills of Kathlog, Potreyn, Terah, Bakrota and Bhangora, Dalhousie is popular hill station that was founded by Lord Dalhousie
Rich in colonial architecture, the town preserves some beautiful churches. A veneer of Tibetan culture has added a touch of the exotic to this serene destination.

DL2.claim: Subhash Chandra Bose stayed in Dalhousie for months in 1937; Subhash Baoli spring and Subhash Chowk are named after him.

evidence.quote: freedom fighter Subhash Chandra Bose stayed on for many months at Dalhousie in 1937. The spring water fed Subhash Baoli and Subhash Chowk are named after him.

DL3.claim: The Mall Road is the place for Himachali shawls, Chamba rumals, traditional jewellery and Tibetan handicrafts.

evidence.quote: The Mall Road is a good place to shop for woollen Himachali shawls, Chamba rumals, traditional jewellery, Tibetan handicrafts and other items.

DL4.claim: Pathankot station is 87 km away and Gaggal (Kangra) airport 110 km; buses run to Pathankot, Amritsar, Delhi, Shimla, Chamba and Bharmaur.

evidence.quote: Rail: Nearest train station to Dalhousie is Pathankot, 87 km away.
The nearest domestic airport to Dalhousie is Gaggal Airport ( Kangra) which is 110 km away.
Public and private transport services are available for Pathankot, Amritsar, Delhi, Shimla and other cities. There are regular bus services for Chamba, Bharmaur and other destinations.
Dalhousie is 54 km from Chamba.

DL6.claim: St. John's (1863) is the oldest church, St. Francis (1894) has Belgian glass, and St. Patrick's (1909) is the largest.

evidence.quote: The oldest church in town, St. John’s Church was built in 1863
The St. Francis Church, a Catholic Church built in the year 1894
the St. Patrick’s Church, largest of all the churches in Dalhousie. Built in the year 1909

DL7.claim: Panjpula, 6 km out, is a stream confluence crossed by five bridges; the Satdhara falls on the way are best in July–August.

evidence.quote: Scenic Panjpula, 6 km from Dalhousie, is a confluence of mountain streams whose waters are believed to have medicinal properties.
Over these streams are five bridges built, giving the place its name.
The waterfall is a place to be at during monsoon season in July – August, when the water gushes at its prime.

DL8.claim: A 5 km uphill walk through deodar, pine and oak forest leads to Bakrota Hill.

evidence.quote: The 5 km uphill walk to Bakrota Hill passes through the natural splendor of Dalhousie dominated by thick deodar, pine and oak forests

DL9.claim: Many of Dalhousie's restaurants are on Thandi Sadak and Garam Sadak.

evidence.quote: Some of the finest restaurants and places to dine are located on the Thandi Sadak and Garak Sadak in Dalhousie.

DL10.claim: Most sights are reached on foot along the town's paths; taxis and buses cover the rest.

evidence.quote: To enjoy a stay in Dalhousie, it is best to commute by walking through the pathways to all scenic spots that can be easily reached. Taxis are readily available for all places of interest.

DL11.claim: Dalhousie has a government Civil Hospital, a Military Hospital and private clinics.

evidence.quote: There is a government Civil Hospital, a Military Hospital and well run private clinics

DL12.claim: Summer is the best time for Dalhousie and Khajjiar — clear skies from March to June — while winters are cold with heavy snow.

evidence.quote: Summer is the best time to be in Dalhousie and Khajjiar. Spring breaks out in March and till June the skies are usually clear
Winters are cold as the hill stations does receive heavy rounds of snow.

DL13.claim: All national mobile networks work in Dalhousie and internet is good.

evidence.quote: All national mobile phone companies provide services in Dalhousie. Internet connectivity is good in town and at nearby tourist places.

DL14.claim: Khajjiar is a wide meadow around a pond, ringed by cedar forest, with the 12th-century Khajji Nag temple nearby.

evidence.quote: Often compared with Swiss mountain meadows, Khajjiar is a wide grassy clearing around a pond with a thick cedar forest.
A few meters from the pond is the temple of Khajji Nag that dates back to the 12th century AD.

DL15.claim: Khajjiar is 22–23 km from Dalhousie and 24–26 km from Chamba; an easy trek also comes up from Chamba.

evidence.quote: This scenic spot is 24 km from Chamba and 22 km from Dalhousie.
This scenic spot is 26 km from Chamba and 23 km from Dalhousie.
an easy trek to Khajjiar from Chamba brings you up close with nature

DL16.claim: The Chamera dam lake on the Ravi, 25 km from Dalhousie, offers boating, kayaking, canoeing and sailing.

evidence.quote: Water sport activities of boating, kayaking, canoeing, sailing and fishing are recreational
The Chamera dam built on River Ravi is 25 km from Dalhousie.

DL17.claim: Dainkund (2,755 m) is the highest hill around Dalhousie; a side road from 13 km along the Khajjiar road leads up.

evidence.quote: Dainkund is the highest mountain among the hills around Dalhousie. From an altitude of 2755 meters the views are wide
a diverting road from an intersection at 13 km from Dalhousie on the road to Khajjiar leads to Diankund peak.

DL18.claim: Kalatop Wildlife Sanctuary, 13 km from Dalhousie, shelters Himalayan black bear, leopard, goral and monal; winter snow can be over five feet deep.

evidence.quote: Sheltered wildlife found in the sanctuary are the Himalayan black bear, leopard, ghoral deer, monal pheasant and others.
winters can pound Kalatop with heavy snow that at times can pile to a heap of over five feet. Kalatop is 13 km from  Dalhousie

DL19.claim: English and Hindi are understood in the tourism trade.

evidence.quote: People engaged in tourism trade understand and communicate in English and Hindi.

CB1.claim: Chamba was founded in 920 AD by Raja Sahil Varman, who moved his capital from Bharmaur at the wish of his daughter Champavati.

evidence.quote: the sprawling township of Chamba was founded by Raja Sahil Varman in 920 AD
It was at the insistence of his daughter Champavati that the king shifted his capital from Bharmaur to Chamba.

CB2.claim: Chamba sits on terraces on the right bank of the Ravi where the Sal river joins it.

evidence.quote: Nestling on the right bank of River Ravi, on terraced flats at a scenic place where the smaller Sal River meets the large one

CB3.claim: Chamba's heritage includes temple architecture, miniature paintings and the embroidered Chamba rumal.

evidence.quote: A splendid artistic heritage includes fine temple architecture, beautiful miniature paintings and the exquisite embroidered Chamba Rumal.

CB4.claim: A Himachali folk song tells you to settle not in Shimla or Kasauli but to visit Chamba for sure.

evidence.quote: Settle not in Shimla, not in Kasauli, visit Chamba for sure

CB5.claim: Summer can reach about 35°C and winter nears 0°C; the climate makes Chamba a year-round destination.

evidence.quote: Summer temperature in Chamba can rise to around 35 degree Celsius and in winter they do hover near Zero degree Celsius.
Chamba for its moderate climate is a year around destination.

CB6.claim: Pathankot airport and railway station are about 120 km away and Gaggal airport 150 km; buses run to Shimla, Chandigarh, Delhi, Dharamshala, Dalhousie and Bharmaur.

evidence.quote: The nearest airport to Chamba is the Pathankot Airport, at a distance of 120 km. The other closest airport is at Gaggal, Kangra, which is at a distance of 150 km from Chamba.
Nearest railway station is Pathankot, about 120 km from Chamba.
Private and public transport networks operate services to the major cities of Dharamshala, Shimla, Mandi, Kullu, Chandigarh, Delhi and to nearby stations of Bharmaur and Dalhousie.

CB7.claim: The Chaugan is Chamba's central grassy ground for picnics, sports and festivals, and hosts the Minjar fair.

evidence.quote: The nerve centre of Chamba, Chaugan is a grassy open area, ideal for leisure, picnics and holding of sporting events.
The Chaugan plays host to the annual Minjar Mela.

CB8.claim: The 300-year-old stone and wood Chamunda Devi temple overlooks the town, reached by steps from the old bus stand or by road.

evidence.quote: Overlooking the town, the stone and wood temple of Chamunda Devi is over 300 years old.
It can be reached by a stairway from the old bus stand as well as by a car from an alternate route.

CB9.claim: The Lakshmi Narayan complex has six shikhara temples; the main one, to Vishnu, was built by the town's founder Raja Sahil Varman.

evidence.quote: consisting of 6 temples is a landmark of the historical town
The main temple, dedicated to Lord Vishnu, was built by Raja Sahil Varman who founded the town.
Interestingly three of these temples are dedicated to Lord Shiva and one to Radha Krishna.

CB10.claim: The Bhuri Singh Museum, set up in 1908, displays miniature paintings, coins, jewellery, arms and copper-plate inscriptions.

evidence.quote: Raja Bhuri Singh, a former ruler of Chamba in his lifetime (1908 AD) did set up this museum that has a fine collection of rare paintings, coins, jewellery, musical instruments, artefacts, traditional arms & armours
There are also some rare copper-plate inscriptions and other historical documents preserved in this museum.

CB11.claim: Minjar, Chamba's main festival, runs for a week on the Chaugan in July/August with craft stalls and evening cultural shows.

overview.text:
Dharamshala sits in the shadow of the Dhauladhar range, 18 km uphill from Kangra. The town has two halves: Lower Dharamshala, around Kotwali Bazar and its markets, and the upper reaches of pine, cedar and oak forest around McLeodganj.

McLeodganj, at 2,082 m, is the seat of the Tibetan Government in exile and home of the 14th Dalai Lama since he left Lhasa after the 1959 uprising — which is why it is often called Little Lhasa. Above it, Dharamkot is the starting point for the Triund trek. Lower down are the Kangra Art Museum, the War Memorial and, a short drive away, Norbulingka Institute, the Gyuto Monastery, the Chamunda Devi temple and Kangra Fort.

best_time.text:
Himachal Tourism recommends March to June and December to February — winter brings a good chance of snow. Lower Dharamshala is warmer in summer, while the upper town around McLeodganj gets very cold in winter, so pack for both.

In the July–August monsoon, mountain roads get slippery and landslides happen, though the Bhagsunag waterfall is at its fullest from July to September. The Dal fair is held in Upper Dharamshala in August.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Kangra airport at Gaggal is 13–14 km from Dharamshala, with regular flights from Delhi.

By train: the nearest broad-gauge station is Pathankot, about 95 km away; from there the narrow-gauge Kangra valley line runs to Kangra station, 20 km from Dharamshala.

By bus: public and private buses run to Delhi, Chandigarh, Pathankot, Kullu-Manali and Shimla. HRTC and HPTDC buses can be booked online on their websites.

By car: one route from Delhi runs via Ambala, Ropar, Una and Kangra; taxis are easy to find for onward trips.

local_transport.text:
Taxis go everywhere around Dharamshala — hire authorised taxis and ask for the government-approved fare chart. McLeodganj, Bhagsu and Dharamkot are close enough to walk between, and the Bhagsunag temple is 2 km from McLeodganj.

Driving yourself: use the public car parks — Hotel Bhagsu car park, the McLeodganj car park and the Community Hall parking in Kotwali Bazar — as McLeodganj's lanes are narrow.

where_to_stay.text:
McLeodganj is the liveliest base, with the Tsuglagkhang, shops and most of the restaurants on the doorstep. Dharamkot and Bhagsu, just above, are quieter and suit trekkers heading for Triund. Lower Dharamshala is handier for the bus stand, Kangra and the airport side.

Wherever you stay, choose hotels, guest houses or homestays registered with the Department of Tourism.

overview.text:
McLeodganj, the upper part of Dharamshala at 2,082 m, is the seat of the Tibetan Government in exile. The 14th Dalai Lama settled here after escaping Lhasa in 1959, and the Tibetans who followed gave the town its nickname, Little Lhasa.

Life centres on the Tsuglagkhang temple complex, with the market wrapped around it. The main street is lined with Tibetan craft shops and eateries whose dishes carry Tibetan flavours. Walks lead in every direction: 2 km to the Bhagsunag temple and waterfall, uphill to Dharamkot — the base for Triund — and 4 km to the deodar-ringed Dal Lake.

overview.text:
Triund is the classic Dhauladhar walk: a ridge-top meadow at 2,875 m, just below the snowline, with the white wall of the range right in front of you. Himachal Tourism grades it moderate. The trail climbs from Dharamkot, above McLeodganj, through thick oak and deodar forest scattered with rhododendrons; the last stretch is the hardest, up 22 steep bends to an open camping ground. The walk down is easy.

Triund is also the gateway to longer treks: the demanding Indrahar Pass (4,342 m), crossed from April to October, starts from Galu Devi Temple near Dharamkot.

overview.text:
Kangra Fort, built by the Katoch rulers, is one of the largest and oldest forts in the Himalayas. Also known as Nagarkot, it stands on high ground protected on three sides by the Banganga river and another stream, which kept it among the strongest forts through its history. The devastating earthquake of 1905 caused extensive damage, but much of the stonework survives.

The fort is about 3 km from Kangra town, and a museum at the entrance has old photographs of the fort before the earthquake. Kangra itself is 10 km from Gaggal airport and on the Pathankot–Joginder Nagar narrow-gauge line, and Dharamshala is an 18 km drive uphill.

overview.text:
Bir, a village among tea gardens in the Kangra valley, is a playground for paragliders and is known for its Buddhist monasteries and Tibetan handicrafts. Himachal Tourism calls Bir-Billing one of the best aero-sports sites in the world; it has hosted the paragliding world cup, and cross-country pilots fly routes of over 200 km.

Flights launch from the meadow at Billing, 14 km above Bir at about 2,400 m, and land at Chowgan on the southern edge of Bir, where most of the stays are. Below the landing field is the Bir Tibetan Colony, founded in the early 1960s, with Chokling monastery's large stupa; Sherab Ling monastery and the cooperative Bir Tea Factory are nearby.

places.name: Palampur
places.summary: The tea capital of North India: a plateau town of tea estates below the Dhauladhars, near Baijnath, Andretta and Bir-Billing.

overview.text:
Palampur, 35 km from Kangra, is a quiet town on a plateau with the Neugal chasm on one side and tea estates and pine and deodar forests all around. Known as the tea capital of North India, it lives by its gardens, where you can learn how tea is made and brewed. Trails into the hills are used by the Gaddi shepherds.

Palampur makes a calm base for the eastern Kangra valley: the 13th-century Baijnath temple is 16 km away, Andretta's art gallery and pottery 13 km, Dhauladhar Nature Park 15 km and Bir-Billing's paragliding about 35 km.

best_time.text: Summers in Palampur are hot and winters quite cold, so pack cottons for summer and heavy woollens for winter. The Holi fair is in February–March, and Baijnath's Shivratri fair draws thousands of pilgrims. In July–August, mountain roads get slippery with landslides.

how_to_reach.text:
By bus: buses run from Dharamshala, Kangra, Kullu and Shimla.

By train: Palampur is on the narrow-gauge Pathankot–Joginder Nagar line.

Around town: local buses run regularly and taxis are available.

overview.text:
The stone temple of Baijnath, 16 km from Palampur, was rebuilt at an older temple site by two local merchants in 1204 AD. The shikhara-style temple enshrines a Shiva linga, and believers hold that Ravana himself meditated here.

At Shivratri the temple is draped in flower garlands and a fair draws thousands of pilgrims. Baijnath lies on the highway towards Bir-Billing, so the two combine easily in a day.

overview.text:
Dalhousie spreads over five hills — Kathlog, Potreyn, Terah, Bakrota and Bhangora — and was founded by Lord Dalhousie as a summer retreat. It keeps its colonial churches and a touch of Tibetan culture, with forest trails looking out over wooded hills, waterfalls and the Ravi winding below, and the snow-capped Dhauladhars on the horizon. Subhash Chandra Bose stayed here for months in 1937; the Subhash Baoli spring and Subhash Chowk are named after him.

Most sights are a walk away, and Khajjiar's meadow, Dainkund peak, Kalatop sanctuary and the Chamera lake make easy excursions. Chamba is 54 km away.

best_time.text: Summer is the best time for Dalhousie and Khajjiar: spring arrives in March and until June the skies are usually clear and temperatures moderate. local_transport.text: Dalhousie is a walking town: the scenic spots are linked by pathways. Taxis are available for every sight and buses serve most places. Hire authorised taxis and ask for the government fare chart.

where_to_stay.text: Staying near the Mall Road and Gandhi Chowk puts the churches, shops and restaurants within walking distance. For quiet and views, stay towards the forest roads, or overnight at Khajjiar to see the meadow early. Choose places registered with the Department of Tourism.

places.name: Khajjiar
places.summary: A wide meadow around a pond, ringed by cedar forest, with the 12th-century Khajji Nag temple — often compared to Switzerland.

images.alt: The green meadow of Khajjiar surrounded by tall cedar trees
images.caption: Khajjiar meadow

overview.text:
Often compared with Swiss mountain meadows, Khajjiar is a wide grassy clearing around a pond, ringed by thick cedar forest. A few metres from the pond stands the Khajji Nag temple, dating to the 12th century AD.

Khajjiar is 22–23 km from Dalhousie and 24–26 km from Chamba; an easy trek also comes up from Chamba. The higher hills around it form the Kalatop Wildlife Sanctuary, and the side road to Dainkund peak leaves the Dalhousie–Khajjiar road at 13 km. Like Dalhousie, it is at its best from March to June.

how_to_reach.text: By road from Dalhousie (22–23 km) or Chamba (24–26 km); taxis are easy to hire in both towns. Walkers can take the easy trek up from Chamba.

items.body: Arrive early for the quiet meadow before day-trippers.
Combine with Dainkund peak on the way from Dalhousie.
Carry warm layers — the meadow is cold in the evenings outside summer.

overview.text: Overlooking the grasslands of Khajjiar, Dainkund is the highest mountain among the hills around Dalhousie. From 2,755 m the views are wide — a photographer's favourite. A side road leaves the Dalhousie–Khajjiar road at an intersection 13 km from Dalhousie and climbs to the peak.

overview.text: The higher hills of Khajjiar form the Kalatop Wildlife Sanctuary, 13 km from Dalhousie — good for forest walks and treks. Himalayan black bear, leopard, goral and monal pheasant live here. Summers are pleasant, but winter snow can pile up more than five feet deep.

overview.text: Panjpula, 6 km from Dalhousie, is a confluence of mountain streams crossed by five bridges — hence the name — and a pleasant picnic spot. On the way, the Satdhara falls are formed by seven spring streams and gush strongest in the monsoon, July–August. Keep off wet rocks by the water.

places.name: Chamba
places.summary: A 10th-century royal town on the Ravi with stone temples, the Chaugan, miniature art and the Chamba rumal — gateway to Bharmaur and Manimahesh.
places.seoTitle: Chamba travel guide: temples, Minjar fair, how to reach

images.alt: Chamba town on terraces above the Ravi river
images.caption: Chamba and the Ravi

overview.text:
A popular Himachali folk song advises: settle not in Shimla, not in Kasauli, but visit Chamba for sure. The town sits on terraces on the right bank of the Ravi, where the Sal river joins it. Raja Sahil Varman founded it in 920 AD, moving his capital from Bharmaur at the wish of his daughter Champavati.

Chamba keeps much of its medieval past: the six stone temples of the Laxmi Narayan complex, the Chamunda Devi temple above the town, the Bhuri Singh Museum and the Chaugan, its grassy heart. Its artistic heritage includes miniature paintings and the embroidered Chamba rumal. Khajjiar is 24–26 km away and Bharmaur, with its Chaurasi temples, 65 km.

places.name: Laxmi Narayan temples
places.summary: Chamba's landmark complex of six stone shikhara temples, the main one to Vishnu built by the town's founder.
places.seoDescription: Chamba's Laxmi Narayan complex: six stone shikhara temples to Vishnu, Shiva and Radha Krishna, built from the 10th century.

images.commons: File:Closer view of architecture of Laxminarayan temple, Chamba 03.jpg
images.alt: Carved stone shikhara towers of the Laxmi Narayan temples in Chamba
images.caption: Laxmi Narayan temples

overview.text:
The Lakshmi Narayan complex is Chamba's landmark: six shikhara-style stone temples capped with circular slate-roofed chhatris on wooden beams. The main temple, to Vishnu, was built by Raja Sahil Varman, who founded the town in 920 AD; three of the others are to Shiva and one to Radha Krishna.

Look closely at the chiselled stone walls, carved with intricate designs, and the small arches on carved pillars framing sculpted deities. The complex is a short walk from the Chaugan.

items.body: Come in the soft morning or late-afternoon light, when the carved stone shows best.
Walk on to the Chaugan and the Bhuri Singh Museum — all three are close together.
Dress modestly and remove shoes before entering the shrines.

places.name: Chaugan
places.summary: Chamba's grassy central ground: picnics, sports and the Minjar fair.
places.seoDescription: The Chaugan, Chamba's grassy centre and home of the Minjar fair.

overview.text: The Chaugan is the nerve centre of Chamba: a grassy open space for leisure, picnics and sports, and the town's stage for festivals, including the annual Minjar fair in July/August. Eateries, including the Chaugan Restaurant, are scattered around it, and the Laxmi Narayan temples are a short walk away.

places.name: Bhuri Singh Museum
places.summary: Chamba's museum, founded in 1908, with miniature paintings, coins, jewellery, arms and copper-plate inscriptions.
places.seoDescription: Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba: royal miniatures, coins, arms and copper-plate inscriptions since 1908.

overview.text: Raja Bhuri Singh, a former ruler of Chamba, set up this museum in 1908. It shows rare paintings — including the royal family's miniatures — coins, jewellery, musical instruments, traditional arms and armour, and rare copper-plate inscriptions. Hours and fees aren't confirmed by an official source.

places.name: Minjar fair
places.summary: Chamba's main festival: a week on the Chaugan in July/August with craft stalls and evening performances.
places.seoDescription: The Minjar fair in Chamba: a week-long July/August harvest festival on the Chaugan.

overview.text: Minjar, the main festival of Chamba, is held on the Chaugan in July/August. Farmers pray for a good harvest by offering the first corn silk — 'minjar' — to the Ravi. The celebrations last a week, with stalls selling local crafts and produce and evening cultural performances that draw big crowds.

places.name: Bharmaur
places.summary: Chamba's old capital between the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal, with the 84 Chaurasi temples and the start of the Manimahesh Yatra.
places.seoDescription: Bharmaur, 65 km from Chamba: the 7th-century Chaurasi temples, Gaddi culture, and the base for the Manimahesh Yatra.

images.alt: Stone and wooden temples of the Chaurasi complex in Bharmaur
images.caption: Chaurasi temples

overview.text:
Bharmaur was the seat of power for four centuries before the capital moved to Chamba. It lies by the Budhal river in a fertile valley between the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal ranges, home to the nomadic Gaddi herders.

In the heart of town, the Chaurasi complex dates back to the 7th century: 84 temples and shrines dedicated to 84 yogis, the main one to Shiva as Mani Mahesh. Bharmaur is 65 km from Chamba and the base for the Manimahesh Yatra in August–September; the mountaineering institute also runs a centre here with camps in climbing, mountaineering and skiing.

how_to_reach.text: Bharmaur is 65 km from Chamba by road; buses run between them, and Dalhousie also has regular buses to Bharmaur. Pathankot (about 120 km beyond Chamba) is the nearest railway station and airport.

places.name: Manimahesh Yatra

places.seoDescription: The Manimahesh Yatra: an arduous August–September pilgrimage trek to the 4,190 m lake, with a six-day Gaddi fair at Bharmaur.

overview.text: The Manimahesh Yatra is held in August–September, after Janmashtami. It is an arduous trek to a mountain lake at 4,190 m at the foot of Mount Kailash. At Bharmaur, 35 km short of the lake, the Gaddi people hold a six-day fair. Prepare as for any high-altitude trek: tell the authorities and use registered guides.
